ukmt-sk-2015-01.title: Gold coins stay fixed
ukmt-sk-2015-01.body:
There are $0.02\times200=4$ gold coins, and this number never changes. In the final pile they are $20\%$, so the final pile has $4\times5=20$ coins. Simon removes $200-20=180$ silver coins.

**Answer: 180**

ukmt-sk-2015-01.title: Solve an equation
ukmt-sk-2015-01.body:
After $s$ days the pile has $200-s$ coins and $4$ of them are gold: $4=0.2(200-s)$, so $200-s=20$ and $s=180$.

**Answer: 180**

ukmt-sk-2015-02.title: Simplify from the inside
ukmt-sk-2015-02.body:
$1+\frac15=\frac65$, so $\frac{1}{1+1/5}=\frac56$. Then $1+\frac56=\frac{11}6$, so the next fraction is $\frac6{11}$, and $1+\frac6{11}=\frac{17}{11}$. Since $\gcd(17,11)=1$, $a+b=17+11=28$.

**Answer: 28**

ukmt-sk-2015-03.title: Compare faces
ukmt-sk-2015-03.body:
Call the three unknown vertices $x,y,z$ (with $z$ the lowest vertex). Three faces meet at the vertex $1$ and contain the vertices $\{1,5,x\}$, $\{1,x,y\}$, $\{1,5,y\}$. Equal sums give $x=y=5$, so every face sum is $1+5+5=11$. The bottom face contains $x,y,z$, so $x+y+z=11$.

**Answer: 11**

ukmt-sk-2015-04.title: Pigeonhole
ukmt-sk-2015-04.body:
Six socks are not enough: they could be the three socks with holes plus one hole-free sock of each colour, giving no hole-free pair.

Seven socks are enough: at most $3$ of them have holes, so at least $4$ are hole-free, and with only $3$ colours two of those four have the same colour.

**Answer: 7**

ukmt-sk-2015-05.title: Use the diagonal
ukmt-sk-2015-05.body:
Let $O$ be the centre of the large circle (radius $10$, the side of the square) and $Q$ the opposite corner of the square, so $OQ=10\sqrt2$. Let the small circle have radius $r$ and centre $P$. It is tangent to the two sides through $Q$, so $P$ lies on diagonal $OQ$ with $PQ=r\sqrt2$. The circles touch externally, so $OP=10+r$. Hence
$$10+r+r\sqrt2=10\sqrt2\ \Rightarrow\ r=\frac{10(\sqrt2-1)}{\sqrt2+1}=10(\sqrt2-1)^2=30-20\sqrt2.$$
So $a=30$, $b=20$ and $a+b=50$.

**Answer: 50**

ukmt-sk-2015-06.title: Set up the ordered list
ukmt-sk-2015-06.body:
Let the integers be $p\le q\le r\le s\le t$. The median is $r$ and the mode is $r-1$, so the value $r-1$ appears at least twice: $p=q=r-1$ (and no other value repeats, so $r<s<t$). The mean is $r+1$, so the total is $5r+5$:
$$(r-1)+(r-1)+r+s+t=5r+5\ \Rightarrow\ s+t=2r+7.$$
Since $s\ge r+1$, the largest $t$ is $2r+7-(r+1)=r+6$. The range is at most $t-p=(r+6)-(r-1)=7$, and e.g. $r=3$: $2,2,3,4,9$ gives median 3, mode 2, mean 4 and range 7.

**Answer: 7**

ukmt-sk-2015-07.title: Add up the pieces
ukmt-sk-2015-07.body:
Triangle $AST$ is similar to $ABC$ with ratio $2:1$ (since $SA=2BA$, $TA=2CA$), so its area is $4\times12=48$; removing $ABC$ leaves $36$ for the quadrilateral $BSTC$. In the same way the quadrilaterals $CUPA$ and $AQRB$ each have area $36$.

Triangles $APQ$ and $ABC$ are congruent (SAS: $AP=AB$, $AQ=AC$, vertically opposite angles at $A$), so $APQ$ has area $12$; likewise $BRS$ and $CTU$ have area $12$.

The hexagon consists of $ABC$ ($12$), the three quadrilaterals ($3\times36=108$) and the three outer triangles ($3\times12=36$): $12+108+36=156$.

**Answer: 156**

ukmt-sk-2015-08.title: Let the number of greys be $g$
ukmt-sk-2015-08.body:
The $k$-th grey kangaroo is taller than exactly $2k-1$ red kangaroos. The last one ($k=g$) is taller than all the reds, so there are $2g-1$ red kangaroos. Then $g+(2g-1)=2015$, so $3g=2016$ and $g=672$.

**Answer: 672**

ukmt-sk-2015-09.title: Two equations
ukmt-sk-2015-09.body:
Let the large rectangle be $x$ by $y$, cut into four pieces of size $\frac x4$ by $y$. Perimeters: $2x+2y=2\cdot\frac x4+2y+18$, so $\frac{3x}2=18$ and $x=12$. Areas: $xy=\frac x4y+18$, so $12y=3y+18$ and $y=2$. The perimeter is $2(12+2)=28$ m.

**Answer: 28**

ukmt-sk-2015-11.title: Reflect the table
ukmt-sk-2015-11.body:
Instead of bouncing, unfold the path by reflecting the table in each cushion the ball hits. The path becomes a straight segment from $A$ to a reflected copy $B'$ of $B$. Along the path the ball travels $2+1+1+2=6$ m horizontally in total and $2+2=4$ m vertically in total (it goes up the full height of the table once and down once), so the straight unfolded segment has length $\sqrt{6^2+4^2}=\sqrt{52}$ metres.

**Answer: 52**

ukmt-sk-2015-12.title: Time equation
ukmt-sk-2015-12.body:
Planned speed $x-5$, actual speed $x$:
$$\frac{210}{x-5}-\frac{210}{x}=1\ \Rightarrow\ 210\cdot5=x(x-5)\ \Rightarrow\ x^2-5x-1050=0\ \Rightarrow\ (x-35)(x+30)=0.$$
So $x=35$.

**Answer: 35**

ukmt-sk-2015-12.title: Guess and check
ukmt-sk-2015-12.body:
$210=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot7$. Try planned speed 30 and actual speed 35: times $7$ h and $6$ h, a difference of exactly 1 hour. The equation above has only one positive root, so $x=35$.

**Answer: 35**

ukmt-sk-2015-14.title: Count the failures
ukmt-sk-2015-14.body:
The numbers who failed problems 1 to 4 are $10,15,20,25$, a total of $70$. A contestant who fails several problems is counted several times, so at most $70$ contestants fail something, and at least $100-70=30$ solve all four. This is attainable when the groups of failures are disjoint.

**Answer: 30**

ukmt-sk-2015-15.title: Divisibility by 3, 5 and 11
ukmt-sk-2015-15.body:
$165=3\cdot5\cdot11$. Divisible by 5: $Y=0$ or $5$. Divisible by 3: the digit sum $3X+4+Y$ needs $4+Y$ divisible by 3, so $Y=5$. Divisible by 11: alternating digit sum $X-X+4-X+Y=9-X$ must be a multiple of 11, so $X=9$. Check: $99495=165\times603$. Hence $X+Y=14$.

**Answer: 14**

ukmt-sk-2015-16.title: Alternate the middle digit
ukmt-sk-2015-16.body:
A digit 1 or 3 must be followed by 2, while a digit 2 can be followed by 1 or 3. So the digits at odd positions or at even positions are all 2, and the others are free to be 1 or 3. If the first digit is 2, then positions $1,3,5,7,9$ are 2 and positions $2,4,\dots,10$ are free: $2^5=32$ numbers. If the first digit is 1 or 3, positions $2,4,6,8,10$ are all 2 and positions $1,3,5,7,9$ are free but the first must not be 2: $2^5=32$ numbers. Total $32+32=64$.

**Answer: 64**

ukmt-sk-2015-17.title: Similar triangles
ukmt-sk-2015-17.body:
The bisector of the right angle at $J$ makes $N$ equidistant from $JK$ and $JM$; call this distance $x$. Then $KL=x+8$ (the distance of $N$ from $JK$ plus its distance from $LM$).

Triangle $K$-$N$-(foot on $KL$) has legs $x$ and $1$; triangle $N$-$M$-(foot on $LM$) has legs $8$ and $x$ (the vertical leg is the distance from $N$ to the top side, $x$). They are similar since $N$ lies on $KM$, so $\frac1x=\frac x8$, $x=\sqrt8$. Then $KL=8+\sqrt8$, so $a=8$, $b=8$ and $a+b=16$.

**Answer: 16**

ukmt-sk-2015-18.title: Add the three equations
ukmt-sk-2015-18.body:
From $\frac a{b+c}=\frac b{c+a}$ we get $a^2+ac=b^2+bc$, i.e. $(a-b)(a+b+c)=0$. So $a=b$ or $a+b+c=0$; similarly for the other pairs.

If $a+b+c=0$ then $b+c=-a$ and $k=-1$. Otherwise $a=b=c$ and $k=\frac12$. Both occur (e.g. $a=b=c=1$; $a=1,b=2,c=-3$). So there are $2$ values.

**Answer: 2**

ukmt-sk-2015-19.title: Algebra with the diagonal
ukmt-sk-2015-19.body:
Let $AB=x$, $BC=y$, $AC=z$, so $z^2=x^2+y^2=(x+y)^2-2xy=400-4V$ where $V=\frac12xy$ is the area of $ABC$. Triangle $ACD$ is right isosceles with hypotenuse $AC$, so its area is $\frac14z^2=100-V$. The total area is $V+(100-V)=100$.

**Answer: 100**

ukmt-sk-2015-19.title: A special case
ukmt-sk-2015-19.body:
The answer does not depend on the shape, so take the square with $AB=BC=10$: its area is $100$.

**Answer: 100**

ukmt-sk-2015-20.title: Factorise
ukmt-sk-2015-20.body:
$N=(3^8-1)(3^8+1)=(3^4-1)(3^4+1)(3^8+1)=80\cdot82\cdot6562$ and $6562=2\cdot17\cdot193$. So $N=2^4\cdot5\cdot2\cdot41\cdot2\cdot17\cdot193=2^6\cdot5\cdot17\cdot41\cdot193$.

Check $75,\dots,85$: $80=2^4\cdot5$, $82=2\cdot41$ and $85=5\cdot17$ divide $N$. The others fail: $75,78,81,84$ need a factor $3$; $77$ needs $7$; $79$, $83$ are primes not dividing $N$; $76$ needs $19$. The sum is $80+82+85=247$.

**Answer: 247**
